sources.title: First Biennial Transparency Report of the Republic of Serbia
geographic_coverage: areas south of the Sava and Danube rivers
sources.temporal_coverage: Sectoral climate impacts and adaptation reporting through 2024; crop comparison baseline 2011–2020.
sources.methodology: Government BTR compiles sectoral climate-risk and adaptation reports; full English PDF read.
sources.limitations: National self-report; spatial detail varies. The 2014 flood is not attributed to climate change.

sources.title: Programme for Adaptation to Changed Climate Conditions for 2023–2030
sources.organization: Government of the Republic of Serbia; Ministry of Environmental Protection
sources.temporal_coverage: Adaptation programme 2023–2030; first action plan 2024–2026; climate projections through 2081–2100.
sources.methodology: Serbian government programme read in full; English summaries are translated paraphrases.
sources.limitations: Cited studies underpin projections; area shares are not exposed-population estimates.

sources.title: Gender Analysis of the Impact of the 2014 Floods in Serbia
sources.organization: Višnja Baćanović; supported by the OSCE Mission to Serbia
sources.temporal_coverage: Interviews and flood-response observations from May–July 2014; report published 2015.
sources.methodology: Study combines interviews with 78 flood-exposed residents in four municipalities and focus-group input from evacuation-centre volunteers.
sources.limitations: Small event-specific sample; gender-disaggregated administrative records were incomplete. The report does not attribute the flood to climate change.

sources.title: EU for Civil Protection and Disaster Risk Resilience Strengthening in the Republic of Serbia
sources.temporal_coverage: Project ran March 2020–January 2026; page gives no INFORM score reference year.
sources.methodology: Directly read UNDP project-page narrative and impact/status fields.
sources.limitations: Page gives no score vintage or scale and reports project framing rather than evaluated outcomes; INFORM is not an FCV classification.

sources.title: Sustainable Urban and Regional Development Program (SURGE): Annual Report 2025
sources.temporal_coverage: World Bank FY2025 programme activities through June 2025; programme extension ended June 2026.
sources.methodology: World Bank report; read full Serbia chapter and FY2025 results.
sources.limitations: Self-reported FY2025 outputs, not resilience outcomes; programme ended June 2026.

sources.title: Country Climate and Development Report: Western Balkans 6 — Background Note: Adapting to a Changing Climate, the Case for Urgent Action
sources.temporal_coverage: Regional climate-development analysis and cited climate-conflict literature, 2024.
sources.methodology: World Bank regional background note synthesizes climate-risk analysis, regional statistics and cited conflict literature.
sources.limitations: Regional synthesis, not a Serbia-specific causal estimate; the note says a clear causal relationship is not unequivocally established.

claims.locator: BTR printed p. 116, Table 31, agriculture summary.
claims.paraphrase: Maize covers ~45% of arable land, mainly in water-short areas; family farms manage nearly 90% of it and generally have low adaptive capacity. Driest-year yields fell up to 40% against 2011–2020.
claims.limitations: The summary names no maize districts.

claims.locator: BTR printed p. 117, Table 31, fruit-production risk summary.
claims.paraphrase: South of Sava and Danube, apricot and almond face the highest growing-season frost risk; listed fruits cover ~10% of fruit area. Risk is expected high across most Serbia by mid-century.
claims.scenario: Mid-century; no scenario specified in the BTR summary.
geographies: areas south of the Sava and Danube rivers
claims.limitations: Species denominator retained; southern area is not an administrative unit.

claims.locator: BTR printed p. 134, adaptation-programme implementation and financing discussion.
claims.paraphrase: For 2024–2026, RSD 998m was allocated (89.3% national, 10.7% donor); BTR calls funding insufficient and says major monitoring-capacity investment was absent.
claims.limitations: Historical allocation, not actual spending or a future budget.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 22 and 124 (printed p. 125), summary and Appendix P1.3.2/Figure P1.10.
claims.paraphrase: The programme reports high/very-high extreme-precipitation risk on 7% of Serbia in 2001–2020, including central/western Serbia, parts of Vojvodina and eastern Serbia; it projects 56% in 2041–2060 under RCP8.5, citing Životić and Vuković-Vimić (2022).
claims.scenario: The map compares 2001–2020 with 2041–2060 under RCP8.5.
claims.limitations: The source does not locate future hotspots or exposed people/assets.

claims.locator: PDF p. 22, programme summary table, drought entry.
claims.paraphrase: One strong-drought year occurred in 2011–2020; the programme projects 2–3 per decade in 2021–2040, 3–4 in 2041–2060, and 7–8 per decade under RCP8.5 in 2081–2100.
claims.scenario: RCP8.5 for 2081–2100; no scenario specified for nearer periods.

claims.locator: PDF p. 134, Appendix A1.6, recommendations on hazards requiring local risk assessment.
claims.paraphrase: Flood, landslide and erosion risks depend on local terrain and protection works; the programme recommends assessment at local-government level.

claims.locator: Printed pp. 29–30, key findings on emergency information and municipal preparedness.
claims.paraphrase: In the four municipalities studied, the report found no local protection-and-rescue plans, untrained communities, inaudible sirens, no local radio or television guidance, and warnings reaching few people informally.
claims.limitations: Findings are from a small event-specific study and should not be generalized to all Serbian municipalities.

claims.locator: Printed pp. 27 and 32, reception-centre security discussion and key findings/recommendations.
claims.paraphrase: The study identifies older and disabled people, single mothers, women living alone and illiterate residents (mostly women and Roma) as vulnerable; it also notes language barriers for evacuated Roma women.
claims.limitations: The report describes an event-specific sample, not prevalence estimates for these groups nationally.

claims.locator: Printed p. 27, security conditions in large collective/reception centres.
claims.paraphrase: The author warns that isolated, unlit large reception centres without organized support can pose security threats to women because of trafficking, sexual-assault and harassment risks.
claims.limitations: The passage identifies risks, not documented incident counts; the 2014 flood is not climate-attributed.

claims.locator: UNDP project page, opening INFORM discussion.
claims.paraphrase: UNDP reports that INFORM placed Serbia at average score 3.5, medium-risk and rather stable; the page says governance/institutional shortcomings (5.2) and disaster-risk reduction (5.7) undermine coping capacity.
institutions: Serbian disaster risk reduction and emergency management system
claims.limitations: The page gives neither score vintage nor scale; INFORM here is not a conflict or fragility classification.

claims.locator: UNDP project page, DRR-system problem statement, focus and status sections.
claims.paraphrase: UNDP identifies fragmented institutions and procedures plus insufficient central/local prevention, preparedness and response capacity; its project aimed to improve coordination and technical, operational and human capacity and ended in January 2026.
claims.limitations: Project aims are not verified results; the public page offers no subnational breakdown or outcome evaluation.

claims.locator: Printed pp. 88–89, FY2025 GLRC local-support results.
claims.paraphrase: FY2025 began ten green-infrastructure, mobility and climate-resilience space designs across Leskovac, Kragujevac, Užice, Niš and Novi Sad; consultations/gender analysis covered safety and access.

claims.locator: Printed p. 88, Niš and Leskovac urban-planning support results.
claims.paraphrase: Niš analysis recommended narrowing General Urban Plan boundaries to the continuous urban area and reducing construction zones against population/land-use projections; Leskovac planning addressed decline and urban-rural links.
claims.limitations: Climate risk was not assessed in this recommendation.

claims.locator: Printed p. 89, FY2025 national-support results and Užice pilot.
claims.paraphrase: Two draft analyses supported climate integration in a five-year Action Plan for Serbia’s Sustainable Urban Development Strategy; an urban cycling/greenway study launched in Užice.
institutions: Agency for Spatial and Urban Planning
Ministry of Construction, Transport and Infrastructure
claims.limitations: Drafts and pilot, not evaluated outcomes.

claims.locator: Printed p. 22, regional discussion of climate/conflict literature and Western Balkans context.
claims.paraphrase: The World Bank note says evidence suggests climate can multiply conflict risks with agricultural dependence, low development and political marginalization, calling this relevant to Western Balkans historical ethnic tensions and political fragmentation.
claims.limitations: Regional literature synthesis; it offers no Serbia-specific causal estimate and explicitly notes unresolved causality.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Climate may multiply conflict risk alongside agricultural dependence, low development and political marginalization; the note says this is relevant to regional ethnic tensions and political fragmentation.

search_audit.query: Serbia climate change subnational vulnerability regions floods drought heatwaves agriculture official report 2024 PDF
search_audit.outcome: Read the national BTR and adaptation programme; verified south-of-Sava/Danube fruit risk, national drought and precipitation projections, and local flood-study findings from four named municipalities. WB programme report adds named city-level planning examples.

search_audit.query: Serbia climate change conflict security climate security violence displacement primary official report
search_audit.outcome: The World Bank regional note describes a literature-based climate threat-multiplier relationship under specified vulnerabilities and says it is relevant to Western Balkans history, while explicitly noting unresolved causality and offering no Serbia-specific estimate. The 2014 flood report is not climate-attributed.

search_audit.query: Serbia post-conflict environmental legacy climate adaptation displacement local capacity official report
search_audit.outcome: No directly inspected primary source established that conflict or displacement constrained climate adaptation. A UNEP post-conflict cleanup PDF appeared as a lead but returned 403; its snippet was not used as evidence. The accessible plans and programmes document disaster-adaptation capacity, not conflict-mediated effects.

search_audit.query: Serbia local government climate adaptation resilience capacity flood preparedness urban resilience planning early warning
search_audit.outcome: Read UNDP's completed national/local DRR programme summary, Serbia's full adaptation programme, OSCE's local flood study, and the World Bank FY2025 city programme results. The evidence includes identified gaps, programme aims and historical outputs, not evaluated resilience outcomes.

gaps: No directly inspected country-specific primary evidence linked a climate-attributed hazard to armed conflict or organized violence; the OSCE's 2014 flood study documents disaster-emergency protection risks but makes no climate attribution.
A search lead on Serbia's historical post-conflict environmental cleanup could not be read because the UN Digital Library PDF returned 403; no findings were inferred from its indexed snippet.
The adaptation programme's projected precipitation-risk classes are territory shares derived from a cited study; they do not identify exposed people, local assets or realized losses.
The OSCE flood study has a 78-person sample across four municipalities and incomplete gender-disaggregated administrative records; its results are event-specific, not nationally representative.
UNDP does not report the reference year or score scale for the INFORM figures and provides no project outcome evaluation on the public page.
World Bank city-planning examples are historical FY2025 reported outputs; initiated design, draft analyses and recommendations are not completed resilience effects.
